meta.location: The hill Onidah, in the land of Antionum
principles: Looking at what would heal you

world_behind.title: The people ask three questions
world_behind.text: Verse 1 has them wanting one God settled, the planting explained, and a place to start with faith. Alma 32 ended without telling them.

world_behind.title: Alma sends them to the scriptures they already have
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says they ought to search them, and that if they think the scriptures taught them they cannot worship, they have misread. A working question is met with a reading assignment.

world_behind.title: Zenos is a prophet outside our Bible
world_behind.text: He is cited twelve times in this record and nowhere in the King James Bible. The Nephites had his writings on the brass plates, and Jacob 5 preserves his longest piece.

world_behind.title: The Zenos prayer is a list of places
world_behind.text: Wilderness, field, house, closet, congregations, and while cast out. Every location the poor might find themselves in is covered, and none of them is a synagogue.

world_behind.title: Zenock was stoned for saying it
world_behind.text: Verse 17 records the outcome in half a sentence. Alma is telling people who were thrown out of a building about a prophet who was killed, and he does not soften it.

world_behind.title: The brass serpent is introduced as a type
world_behind.text: Verse 19 has Moses raising something in the wilderness so that whoever looked might live. Alma uses it to name the cost of refusing an easy remedy.

world_behind.title: The chapter ends the discourse Alma 32 began
world_behind.text: Verse 23 returns to the seed, the swelling, the nourishing, and the tree, and closes with a promise about lightened burdens.

words.text: A prophet of old whose writings the Nephites carried and the King James Bible does not contain. The record names him twelve times, and Jacob 5 gives his allegory of the olive tree in full. Alma treats him as scripture the Zoramites should already have read.

A small private room. The word occurs twice in this record and twice in the King James Bible, where Christ tells his hearers to enter the closet and shut the door. Zenos names it as one of six places where his prayer was heard.

Assemblies of worshippers, in the plural. It appears once in the record, and three times in the King James Bible, all in the Psalms. Zenos puts public assembly on the same list as a field and a closet, which is the point Alma is building toward.

Freedom from pretense. The record uses it five times and the King James Bible seven. Zenos names his afflictions and his sincerity as the two things God heard, and then says the mercy itself came because of the Son.

A second prophet of old, named five times in this record and never in the King James Bible. Alma quotes one sentence of his and then reports that his people stoned him. Nephi lists him with Isaiah and Jeremiah in Helaman 8.

Lazy, unwilling to stir. The word turns up four times, three of them in Alma 37 about the Liahona, here, and the King James Bible fifteen. Alma applies it to people who will not turn their eyes toward a cure that costs nothing.

phrases.term: Ye ought to search the scriptures
phrases.text: Alma's answer to people asking how to begin. They have a text, and he tells them their reading of it is wrong. Everything that follows in the chapter is him doing the reading with them.

phrases.term: Thou hast heard my prayer, even when I was in the wilderness
phrases.text: The first item in Zenos's list. It begins in the least religious place available and works inward toward the house and the closet, then back out to the congregations.

phrases.term: When I did cry unto thee in my field
phrases.text: A working man praying at work. Alma is quoting this to people who have been told worship happens on a stand once a week, and the field is the strongest example in the list for them.

phrases.term: To be heard of thee and not of men
phrases.text: The line that answers Alma 31 directly. The Rameumptom put one man above every head where all could see; Zenos names being heard by God alone as the point of praying.

phrases.term: Thou hast turned thy judgments away from me, because of thy Son
phrases.text: Alma quotes it and then repeats it in verse 13 as the thing they must believe if they believe Zenos at all. A prophet centuries before Christ attributes God's mercy to the Son.

phrases.term: If ye have read the scriptures, how can ye disbelieve on the Son of God?
phrases.text: Alma puts the Zoramite creed against their own library. Alma 31 had them thanking God that there shall be no Christ; here Alma says the records they possess make that position unavailable.

phrases.term: Because the people would not understand his words they stoned him to death
phrases.text: Zenock's fate, given without comment. Alma is speaking to people who were driven out of a building, and he tells them what happened to a prophet who said what he is now saying.

phrases.term: A type was raised up in the wilderness, that whosoever would look upon it might live
phrases.text: Moses and the brass serpent, named as a type. Alma says many looked and lived. The remedy required one motion and no qualification.

phrases.term: The reason they would not look is because they did not believe that it would heal them
phrases.text: The whole diagnosis in one clause. The refusal was not defiance and not inability; the people did not think it would work. Alma has just told his hearers that the word will work.

phrases.term: Would ye rather harden your hearts in unbelief, and be slothful
phrases.text: Alma's question to the poor. He offers the easiest possible test and names the two things that could stop them: not believing it would help, and not bothering.

phrases.term: Even all this can ye do if ye will
phrases.text: The last sentence of the discourse. After the seed, the prophets, the serpent, and the promise of lightened burdens, Alma ends by saying the whole thing is within reach of the people in front of him.

verses.label: v. 2
verses.title: The objection in their own words
verses.text: The sermon opens by repeating what its hearers have said: "ye have said that ye could not worship your God because ye are cast out of your synagogues." The record could have summarised the difficulty. Instead it puts the claim in the mouths of the people who made it and lets the whole chapter be an answer to that one sentence. Every quotation Alma reaches for afterwards, from Zenos, from Zenock, from Moses, is chosen to meet it, and the last verse returns to the same subject by telling them to plant a word in their hearts instead of in a building.

verses.label: v. 3–11
verses.title: A quotation with none of its frame's vocabulary
verses.text: Zenos's prayer runs from verse 4 to verse 11, and four words live inside it and nowhere else in the chapter: didst seven times, merciful six, hear six, and heard four. The fourteen verses of Alma's own speech that surround it use none of the four. Prayer is the near miss, four times inside the quotation and once outside it, at verse 3, where Alma names the subject he is about to quote on. Of the sixty-seven chapters anywhere in scripture that use merciful at all, this one uses it more than any other, and every instance belongs to the man being quoted, not the man quoting.

verses.label: v. 5–11
verses.title: One sentence, said six ways
verses.text: The record preserves an argument built as a list of places. "Thou didst hear me" closes verse 5, verse 6, verse 7 and verse 11, and the shorter "thou didst hear" also stands in verse 10. Those exact words appear in no other chapter of the volume. What varies between them is only the location: the wilderness, the field, the house, the closet, the congregation, the afflictions. A prayer that could have made its case once makes it six times and changes only the setting.

verses.label: v. 19–20
verses.title: The thing that is never named
verses.text: The third witness is Moses, and the object he raised is left unspecified: "a type was raised up in the wilderness, that whosoever would look upon it might live." The verse does not say serpent, brass, or pole. Verse 20 says only that "few understood the meaning of those things." The volume does name it, once, at Hel. 8:14, "the brazen serpent." Here the noun is withheld and the reader is expected to supply it, which is itself the point verse 20 is making about the people who would not look.

verses.label: v. 21–23
verses.title: The question with a wo attached
verses.text: The sermon ends on a question the hearers are meant to answer against themselves: "if ye could be healed by merely casting about your eyes, would ye not behold quickly, or would ye rather harden your hearts in unbelief?" No other verse in the volume uses the words casting about your eyes, and verse 22 turns the phrase into a command, "cast about your eyes and begin to believe." Between the question and the command sits a threat, "if so, wo shall come upon you," and after them the chapter hands the hearer back the image Alma 32 spent forty verses building: plant the word, nourish it, and it becomes a tree.

chapter.title: The answer to a practical question is a text
chapter.text: The instruction at verse 2 is bibliographic, "ye ought to search the scriptures," and verse 3 is a question about reading, "Do ye remember to have read what Zenos, the prophet of old, has said concerning prayer or worship?" What follows is eight verses of Zenos quoted straight through, then Zenock at verse 16, then Moses at verse 19. Verse 14 puts the whole case as a question about reading, "I would ask if ye have read the scriptures? If ye have, how can ye disbelieve on the Son of God?"

chapter.title: Zenos answers the Rameumptom without mentioning it
chapter.text: Six places where prayer was heard, and none of them a building. Alma never argues against the stand; he reads a prayer that makes it unnecessary.

chapter.title: Being cast out is on the list
chapter.text: Verse 10 has Zenos heard while despised by his enemies. Alma has found a scripture that describes his hearers' exact situation and reports that God answered in it.

chapter.title: He stacks witnesses before he asks for belief
chapter.text: Zenos, Zenock, Moses, and the plain statement that these are not the only ones. The argument is cumulative and it is built entirely out of what the Zoramites already own.

chapter.title: He tells them the last man who said this was killed
chapter.text: Verse 17 sits in the middle of the argument. Alma is asking people who have already paid a price to consider a claim that has cost others more.

chapter.title: The serpent makes refusal look absurd
chapter.text: One glance, no cost, and people died rather than look. Alma converts the doctrine of faith into a question about laziness and disbelief in the cure.

chapter.title: Everything returns to the seed
chapter.text: The chapter opens on the question Alma 32 left and closes on planting and nourishing. The prophets and the serpent are the middle of a single discourse.

chapter.title: The last words are about capacity
chapter.text: The chapter ends on an instruction the hearers can carry out themselves, "plant this word in your hearts, and as it beginneth to swell even so nourish it by your faith." Verse 22 has already given the content to be planted in a single breath, that the Son "shall suffer and die to atone for their sins" and "shall rise again from the dead." The hearers are the people Alma 32:3 describes as "esteemed by their brethren as dross," and the last thing said to them is about what they are able to do.

applications.title: Send people to the text when they ask what to do
applications.text: The answer to a practical question about worship is bibliographic, "ye ought to search the scriptures," followed by "Do ye remember to have read what Zenos, the prophet of old, has said concerning prayer or worship?" A reading assignment is a real answer.

applications.title: Notice where the prayer says he prayed
applications.text: Zenos names six places he prayed in, from open country to a shut room to the middle of an assembly, and not one of them is a temple. Six settings and none of them is a temple. Ask where you have decided prayer belongs, and whether the list is shorter than his.

applications.title: Give the reason the prayer was heard
applications.text: The quoted prayer names it, "thou didst hear me because of mine afflictions and my sincerity; and it is because of thy Son that thou hast been thus merciful unto me." Two things the pray-er brought and one thing he did not.

applications.title: Ask the question that follows from what they already grant
applications.text: "Do ye believe those scriptures which have been written by them of old?" and then "how can ye disbelieve on the Son of God?" The argument moves entirely inside what the hearers have already conceded.

applications.title: Bring the second witness
applications.text: Alma adds Zenock and notes what happened to him, "because the people would not understand his words they stoned him to death." One authority can be dismissed; two of the same kind, one of them killed for it, is a different case.

applications.title: Use the story everybody knows
applications.text: The brass serpent is offered as the example precisely because it is familiar, and the failure is located in effort rather than in ignorance, "because of the simpleness of the way... there were many who perished."

applications.title: Say what to plant, not only that to plant
applications.text: Before the instruction to plant the word, verse 22 states the content in one sentence: that the Son will come to redeem his people, will suffer and die to atone, and will rise. A seed is a specific thing.

applications.title: End on what the hearer can do
applications.text: The last instruction is theirs to carry out, "plant this word in your hearts, and as it beginneth to swell even so nourish it by your faith," addressed to people the society had told were worth nothing.

questions.text: What have I concluded about God from a passage I have not actually read carefully?
Where do I work, and have I ever prayed there?
Am I praying to be heard by God or by the people who might notice?
What in my life has been turned away from me because of the Son?
What true thing am I unwilling to say because of what it might cost?
What remedy do I refuse because I do not believe it would work?
What is the one thing I could do if I would?
